name: Ayoreo
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: One wonders whether the stress is contrastive in Ayoreo. According to Moraire (1980: 1) “the accent falls on the last syllable, except when the word ends in e. In this case the accent falls on the next to the last syllable”. In the orthographic system used by Moraire (1980) and Higham et al. (2000), the accent is indicated when there are exceptions to this rule. [...] According to Bertinetto (2009: 11), one finds possible minimal pairs distinguished by the accent, which generally appears on the last syllable, but the exact location of the accent “seems to vary from speaker to speaker and possibly among the different productions of one and the same speaker”.
new_statements.citation: Ciucci, Luca. 2013. Inflectional morphology in the Zamucoan languages. PhD dissertation, Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa, §2.1 'Ayoreo phonology and orthography', p. 17 (printed page 17 = PDF p. 29). Revised and published as Ciucci 2016, Inflectional morphology in the Zamucoan languages, Asunción: CEADUC (Biblioteca Paraguaya de Antropología 103).
new_statements.locator: p. 17 (§2.1; PDF page 29 of 590); companion first-hand statement Bertinetto 2009: 10-11 (§2.1.3 Prosody) in
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the last syllable of the word; when the word ends in -e (including the paragogic [e] added after a final consonant) it falls on the penultimate syllable. The academic describers (Bertinetto 2009; Ciucci 2010, 2013; Bertinetto, Ciucci & Pia 2010) accept 'generally final' as the tendency but report that placement varies between speakers and even across repetitions by one speaker, note a few candidate minimal pairs, and leave open whether accent is contrastive; an alternative reading would be lexical-unpredictable or unclear-or-contradictory.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Words ending in -e take penultimate accent (Morarie 1980: 1 via Ciucci 2013: 17); Higham et al. (2000) mark the accent orthographically only where it departs from this rule, i.e. there are lexical exceptions. Bertinetto 2009: 11 lists candidate minimal pairs yojí 'my bow' vs yóji 'I drink', pichó '(the fact of) throwing' vs pícho 'wood (base-form plural)' and considers Adelaar's (2004) claim of contrastive stress 'doubtful' but not excluded; Bertinetto, Ciucci & Pia 2010: 14 call the position of lexical accent 'assai oscillante'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical accent of citation forms as recorded by the missionary orthography of Morarie 1980 and Higham et al. 2000); Bertinetto 2009: 10-11 and Ciucci 2010 note 3 describe variation between speakers and between repetitions of the same word by one speaker, and question whether accent is phonologically pertinent. Paragogic [e] after final consonants (dajachuc ~ dajachuque 'boiled', Bertinetto 2009: 11) is what the '-e' exception amounts to: stress stays on the last underlying syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: Ayoreo proper (ayor1240); no separate dialect. Bertinetto's 2009 data come from Bolivian (Santa Cruz area, Tobité mission via Morarie) and Paraguayan communities and he notes only minor North/South (Bolivia/Paraguay) differences (chiefly the realisation of /r/); Ciucci's 2009 fieldwork was in Bolivia and Paraguay. Morarie's rule reflects the Bolivian (Tobité) variety used in the NTM dictionary and Bible translation. Ancient Zamuco (Chomé, 18th c.; Kelm 1964) is a distinct variety with no accent information (Ciucci 2013: 18 fn. 39).

sources.note: §2.1 Ayoreo phonology, p. 17: quotes Morarie (1980: 1) rule 'accent falls on the last syllable, except when the word ends in e; then on the next to the last'; Morarie/Higham et al. orthography marks accent only for exceptions; accent 'generally appears on the last syllable' but location varies between and within speakers (citing Bertinetto 2009: 11; fn. 38: Ciucci observed the same in his own 2009 fieldwork). Also p. 25 for Chamacoco (final in disyllables, penult in longer words, per Ulrich & Ulrich 1989).

sources.citation: Bertinetto, Pier Marco, Luca Ciucci & Gabriella Erica Pia. 2010. Inquadramento storico, etnografico e linguistico degli Ayoreo del Chaco. In Quae omnia bella devoratis. In memoria di Edoardo Vineis, Pisa: ETS, 109-146 (provisional QLL version, 27 pp.).
sources.note: PDF p. 14: "Adelaar parla inoltre di accento contrastivo. Entrambe queste asserzioni ci appaiono prive di riscontro... La posizione dell'accento lessicale, in particolare, appare assai oscillante, tanto da alimentare dubbi circa la sua pertinenza fonologica." Note 25 (p. 7): different speakers produced different accentuations of the same words; 'il problema meriti uno studio adeguato'.

sources.citation: Ciucci, Luca. 2010. La flessione possessiva dell'ayoreo. Quaderni del Laboratorio di Linguistica 9(2): 1-29.
sources.note: Note 3, p. 2: "Per quanto riguada l'accento, non è chiaro se abbia valore fonologico e nel corso delle indagini sul campo si è avuto l'impressione che la sua posizione, entro certi limiti, variasse non soltanto tra parlante e parlante, ma persino mentre il medesimo parlante ripeteva la stessa parola." Accents marked as in Higham et al. (2000).

sources.citation: Bertinetto, Pier Marco. 2009. Ayoreo (Zamuco). A grammatical sketch. Quaderni del Laboratorio di Linguistica della Scuola Normale Superiore 8 n.s. (59 pp.).
sources.note: §2.1.3 Prosody, pp. 10-11: "According to Adelaar (2004), Ayoreo has contrastive stress. Although the present author cannot rule this out, this claim appears to be doubtful. The Ayoreo words are indeed produced with a very perceptible stress prominence (often involving the final syllable); however, its exact location seems to vary from speaker to speaker and possibly among the different productions of one and the same speaker. This topic needs further research." Rejects a stress-less analysis; candidate minimal pairs yojí 'my bow' vs yóji 'I drink', pichó 'throwing' vs pícho 'wood (BF pl.)'; a…
